title: A cooking order without recursion

samples.expect: [flour; water; salt; dough; tomatoes; sauce; pizza]
samples.label: topo (graph [("pizza", ["dough"; "sauce"]); ("dough", ["flour"; "water"; "salt"]); ("sauce", ["tomatoes"; "salt"])]) "pizza"

hints: Keep a stack of `(item, ready)` pairs as a list, starting with `[(root, false)]`, and loop while it isn't empty. Pop by taking the head.
When an item pops without its note: if you've started it already, skip it. Otherwise mark it, then push `(item, true)` and, on top of that, its parts with `false`, the first part at the very top.
When an item pops with its note, all its parts are written, so add it to the output. Build the output backwards with `::` and reverse it at the end.

answer.explain: The stack holds the work a recursive walk would keep on the call stack. An item is marked when it is first expanded, so a shared part is expanded once, and it is written only when it pops again with its note, after all its parts: that is post-order. The parts are pushed with the first one on top, so they come out left to right. Nothing recurses, so the 100,000-deep chain is a loop of 200,000 steps.
